newsitem.title: FRANCE: DHL still backing Strasbourg as Rhine hub.
newsitem.headline: DHL still backing Strasbourg as Rhine hub.

text.p: By Stuart Todd
DHL Worldwide Express said on Wednesday it was still determined to go ahead with its proposed Rhine valley regional air cargo hub at Strasbourg-Entzheim airport despite some strong local opposition.

"Strasbourg remains our firm choice and we are still hopeful of a fourth quarter 1996 start-up. However, if we went into 1997 awaiting a decision, the chances are our plans would be put under serious review," DHL Aviation's business development manager, Steven Lewis, told Reuters from Brussels.

Although 20,000 protest signatures have been collected in recent weeks against the hub according to local sources, the Strasbourg chamber of commerce -- which runs the airport -- as well as the local urban community council have already said they are in favour.
The chamber of commerce told Reuters today that it has so far received around 1,000 letters from companies in the Alsace region supporting the hub.

Lewis said: "The opposition is probably the most significant we have encountered in setting up our European hubs, but we remain committed to getting our case across to the French civil aviation authority, to experts drawing up an impact study and to local residents."

The project made public in late July involves investing $5 million in an initial three to four year phase together with 350 new jobs. This would be followed by further investment in purpose-built facilities costing $50 million as traffic rose.
The local protests, chiefly centred on the potential disturbance caused by late-night and early morning flights, resulted in Strasbourg's mayor Catherine Trautmann commissioning an impact study.

This will be undertaken by independent experts to assess the noise and environmental impact as well as its economic consequences. The study will be reviewed by the airport's environment committee on September 17.
On August 26, DHL provided the same committee with a 10-page document on all aspects of the proposed hub, Lewis said.
Most of the material in the document had been made public in recent months but DHL wanted to clarify the situation, he added.

These included giving assurances "that new jobs would be permanent ones, that aircraft used at Strasbourg meet tough international rules on engine noise and also that DHL was not looking at Strasbourg as a replacement for its Brussels (hub)," Lewis said.

This week, DHL would provide the French civil aviation authority with details on measures to limit aircraft noise and would also meet the independent experts looking into the project's economic consequences, he added.
DHL had invited the French national press and the local Alsace press to visit its hub facilities in Copenhagen to demonstrate the scope that exists to combat noise from aircraft, Lewis said.
"While there are differences between the Copenhagen hub location and the proposed site in Strasbourg, at Copenhagen our aircraft do fly over a populated area," he added.

"The kind of measures we have adopted to minimise noise - varying take-off patterns, deviating flight paths and cutting aircraft engines as soon as possible on landing and transferring to ground power units -- would be envisaged at Strasbourg," he said.

DHL had also twice invited various groups, including local mayors, the urban community council, the chamber of commerce and environmental protection groups to visit its hub facilities. But so far there had been little or no interest shown in the invitation, Lewis added.
DHL plans to begin with one or two nightly flights at Strasbourg Airport using Convair and Electra aircraft -- rising to seven flights nightly in 1997.
The flights would link Strasbourg with its European hub at Brussels and the express distribution group's regional hubs at U.K. East Midlands, Copenhagen, Nuremberg, Cologne, Bergamo and Vittoria.
Deutsche Lufthansa AG and Japan Airlines Co Ltd each hold a 25 percent stake in DHL.
